x-m-fill-b-01.title: Is 'they don't affect each other' really independence?
x-m-fill-b-01.topic: Multiplication rule of probability and independence/dependence
x-m-fill-b-01.goal: Judge whether two events are independent by comparing probability values, not by intuition, and make independent data yourself.
x-m-fill-b-01.material: A box has 3 red balls and 2 blue balls. You take out one ball, check its color, and without putting it back in the box, take out another. Minsu said, 'The event that the first is red and the event that the second is red don't affect each other, so the probability that both are red is 3/5 × 3/5 = 9/25.' (3/5 is read as 'three fifths.')
x-m-fill-b-01.thinking.0: Check a claim with probability values
x-m-fill-b-01.thinking.2: Explain your reason for a judgment in words
x-m-fill-b-01.prereq.0: The meaning of event and probability
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.prompt: What comparison best tests whether Minsu is right?
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.hint.0: You can judge 'there is an effect / there is no effect' by putting two probability values side by side.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.hint.1: Write down how the balls left in the box differ for the two cases of the first ball's color.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.o.a: Find out whether the probability that the second is red is 3/5
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.r.a: The probability of the second ball alone is indeed 3/5. But this alone doesn't show how it relates to the first result.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.o.b: Count how many orders there are for taking the balls in all
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.r.b: Counting all the possible cases is good preparation, but you need to compare separately to know whether the two events affect each other.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.o.c: Compare the probability that the second is red when the first is red and when the first is blue
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.r.c: You are testing the effect directly by looking at whether the second ball's probability stays the same when the first result changes.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.o.d: Check again that 3 of the 5 balls are red
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.r.d: That checks the contents of the box at the start. It doesn't yet look at how the box changes after a ball is taken out.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s1.explain: If the first is red, 2 of the remaining 4 are red, so the probability that the second is red is 2/4. If the first is blue, 3 of the remaining 4 are red, so it is 3/4. It changes depending on the first result, so they are not independent.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.prompt: In the same way, a class of 20 students was surveyed. Event A is 'a student who wears glasses,' and event B is 'a student who joined an after-school class.' With a students in A, b students in B, and c students in both, make 3 different cases where A and B are independent. (a and b are from 1 to 19 students, c is at least 1 student.)
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.hint.0: First write the proportion of students in A and the proportion of students in B as fractions.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.hint.1: The proportion of A students among the B students must be equal to the proportion of A students in the whole class.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.hint.2: After choosing a and b, find c and check that it is an integer.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.var.c: Number of students in both A and B
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The number of students is an integer from 1 to 19.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.fail.c1: a and b must be integers from 1 to 19. (c is also an integer)
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.ok.c2: c is within the possible range.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.fail.c2: c cannot be greater than a or b, and to not go over 20 students it must be at least a+b−20.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.fail.c3: With these numbers, P(A∩B) and P(A)×P(B) are not equal. They are not independent.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s2.explain: If they are independent, (proportion of students in both A and B) = (proportion of A) × (proportion of B). Examples: a=10, b=10 gives c=5; a=4, b=10 gives c=2; a=5, b=8 gives c=2. (Swapping a and b counts as the same example.)
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.prompt: Please answer Minsu. In the box problem, are the two events independent or not? Write the probability values and explain your reason.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write in your own words a comparison of the probabilities in the two cases.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write down the number of balls left when the first is red and when the first is blue.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you show with numbers that the probability the second is red changes depending on the first result?
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you compare the probability that both are red in two ways?
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about 'what happens if the ball is put back'?
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.model.0: They are not independent. Because the ball is not replaced, the probability that the second is red is 2/4 if the first is red, but it changes to 3/4 if the first is blue. The probability that both are red is also 3/5×2/4=3/10=0.3, which differs from 3/5×3/5=0.36.
x-m-fill-b-01.s.s3.model.1: They are dependent. When a ball is taken out, the balls left change, so the second probability changes. It is 1/2 if the first is red and 3/4 if it is blue, but if they were independent these two would have to be equal.

x-m-fill-b-02.title: Does a high score mean you did relatively well?
x-m-fill-b-02.goal: Standardize scores from different tests to compare them, and explain how the judgment changes as data is added.
x-m-fill-b-02.material: On this test, Sujin got 78 in Korean and 84 in math. The scores of each test are considered close to a normal distribution. Part of the standard normal distribution table is as follows: P(0 ≤ Z ≤ 0.7) = 0.2580, P(0 ≤ Z ≤ 1.3) = 0.4032. (Z is a random variable that follows a normal distribution with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.)
x-m-fill-b-02.thinking.0: Revise a judgment as data increases
x-m-fill-b-02.thinking.1: Consider the mean and the spread together
x-m-fill-b-02.thinking.2: Interpret a position with the standard normal distribution table
x-m-fill-b-02.prereq.0: The meaning of normal distribution curve and mean and standard deviation
x-m-fill-b-02.prereq.1: How to read the standard normal distribution table
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. At each step, choose a judgment using only what you know now.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.hint.0: Each time new information appears, think about whether your judgment should change.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether the same score difference means the same thing when the spread of the scores differs.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Sujin's scores are 78 in Korean and 84 in math.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: Which subject do you think Sujin did relatively better in?
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.after: Judging by scores alone, math looks higher. But each test has a different level of difficulty, so it is too early to conclude relative position from this alone.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Math: because the score of 84 is higher
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You compared the size of the scores as they are. This is the first judgment that comes to mind.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Korean: even if the score is lower, Korean must have been harder
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You assumed the test was hard with no basis. We can't know the difficulty of the test right now.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: It is too early to decide from the two scores alone, because each test has its own circumstances
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You saw that more data than the scores is needed.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.info: The means are 65 points in Korean and 70 points in math.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: How does your judgment change after seeing this information?
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.after: The difference from the mean is an important clue, but whether a 14-point difference is big or small depends on how spread out the scores are.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Math: it is 14 points above the mean, 1 point more than Korean (13 points)
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You compared the differences from the mean. It's a step forward, but you haven't yet used how spread out the scores are.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Still too early: without knowing the spread of the scores, you can't compare the values 14 points and 13 points
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You are thinking that the same score difference means something different depending on the spread.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Korean: the mean is lower, so she did better in Korean
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: The fact that the mean is lower does not mean Sujin's position is high.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.info: The standard deviations are 10 points in Korean and 20 points in math.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Finally, which subject do you judge Sujin did relatively better in?
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Korean is (78−65)÷10=1.3, and math is (84−70)÷20=0.7. Looking at how many standard deviations she is from the mean, Korean is the higher position.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Math: it is 14 points above the mean, so it is a higher position than Korean (13 points)
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Even though the standard deviation information appeared, you compared only score differences. Two tests with different spreads do not have the same scale.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Korean: the difference from the mean is 1.3 times the standard deviation and in math it is 0.7 times, so Korean is the higher position
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You divided the difference from the mean by the standard deviation and compared them on the same scale.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Both are above the mean, so she did about equally well
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You only saw that it is above the mean. You did not tell apart how high the position is.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s1.reflect: At first math looked higher, but as the mean and the standard deviation were added, the judgment changed. To compare different tests, you must convert the scores into 'how many standard deviations from the mean' and put them on the same scale.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.prompt: Using the standard normal distribution table, find roughly what percent from the top each of Sujin's two scores is, and interpret the result in one sentence.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.hint.0: First write the value you get by subtracting the mean from each subject's score and dividing by the standard deviation.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.hint.1: The values in the table are the area from the mean (0) up to that value. Think about what to subtract from half of the whole to get the area above.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you first find the standardized values (1.3, 0.7) before reading the table?
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you understand 'subtract the table value from 0.5' along with the reason?
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you interpret by position, not by the size of the score?
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.model.0: Korean has z=1.3, so P(Z≥1.3)=0.5−0.4032=0.0968, about the top 9.7%. Math has z=0.7, so 0.5−0.2580=0.2420, about the top 24.2%. So she did relatively better in Korean.
x-m-fill-b-02.s.s2.model.1: Standardizing gives z=1.3 for Korean and z=0.7 for math. The upper probabilities are 0.0968 (about 9.7%) for Korean and 0.2420 (about 24.2%) for math, so the Korean result is at a higher position within the group.

x-m-fill-b-03.title: If the perimeter is longer, is the area bigger?
x-m-fill-b-03.topic: Comparing perimeter and area of figures
x-m-fill-b-03.goal: Test the statement 'If the perimeter is longer, the area is bigger' with examples, and make several rectangles with the same area to see that perimeter and area are separate.
x-m-fill-b-03.material: Each grid square is a square 1cm wide and 1cm tall. Rectangle 가 is 1 square wide and 9 squares tall. Rectangle 나 is 4 squares wide and 4 squares tall. Jiwoo said, 'A shape with a longer perimeter also has a bigger area.' (가 has a perimeter of 20cm and an area of 9 squares, and 나 has a perimeter of 16cm and an area of 16 squares.)
x-m-fill-b-03.thinking.0: Test with examples whether a statement is always true
x-m-fill-b-03.thinking.1: Find all rectangles that meet a condition
x-m-fill-b-03.prereq.0: The size of one grid square (1cm wide, 1cm tall) and finding area by counting squares
x-m-fill-b-03.prereq.1: What the perimeter of a rectangle is
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.prompt: Looking at 가 and 나, what can you say about Jiwoo's statement?
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.hint.0: Write the perimeter and the area separately and compare the two shapes side by side.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.hint.1: Think about how many examples you need to break 'always true.'
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.o.a: 가 has a longer perimeter and a bigger area, so Jiwoo's statement can be considered true
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.r.a: You compared only the perimeters and did not count the squares for the area. Compare 9 squares and 16 squares again.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.o.b: 가 has a longer perimeter but a smaller area, so Jiwoo's statement can be false
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.r.b: You compared the two values separately and saw 'always' broken by one example.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.o.c: 나 has a shorter perimeter so a smaller area too, so Jiwoo's statement is true in this example
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.r.c: 나's area (16 squares) is bigger than 가's area (9 squares), but you drew a conclusion from the perimeter alone.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.o.d: You can't tell from two shapes whether Jiwoo's statement is true or false
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.r.d: A statement with 'always' can be broken by even one example that doesn't fit. Think about the power of one example.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s1.explain: 가 has a perimeter of 20cm and an area of 9 squares, and 나 has a perimeter of 16cm and an area of 16 squares. The 가 with the longer perimeter has the smaller area, so 'if the perimeter is longer, the area is bigger' is not always true.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s2.prompt: This time, make 3 different rectangles with an area of 12 squares. (a squares wide, b squares tall. Swapping the width and the height counts as the same shape.)
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s2.hint.0: Find the pairs of numbers of squares wide and tall that multiply to 12.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s2.hint.1: Increase the width to 1, 2, 3 squares and check whether the height is a whole number.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s2.ok.c1: The numbers of squares are natural numbers that are at least 1.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s2.fail.c1: The width and the height must be natural numbers at least 1 (a number of squares).
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Width squares × height squares is not 12.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s2.explain: The shapes with an area of 12 squares are three: 1×12, 2×6, and 3×4. (4×3 is the same shape as 3×4.)
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.prompt: Find the perimeter of each of the three rectangles, and write what happens to the perimeter when the area is the same. Also guess which shape gives the shortest perimeter.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.hint.0: The perimeter of each rectangle is (width+height) added twice.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.hint.1: Put the three perimeters side by side and look at which shape gives the smallest.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you find all three perimeters?
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you state your guess with numbers (for example, 3×4)?
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write knowing that it is not true that 'if the area is the same, the perimeter is the same'?
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.model.0: 1×12 has a perimeter of 26, 2×6 has 16, and 3×4 has 14. The area is the same 12 squares, but the perimeters differ. The closer the width and the height are, as in 3×4, the shorter the perimeter.
x-m-fill-b-03.s.s3.model.1: (1,12) gives a perimeter of 26, (2,6) gives 16, (3,4) gives 14. Even with the same area the perimeters can differ, and the perimeter is shortest when the lengths are close, like 3 and 4.

x-m-fill-b-04.title: Can you tell the number of cubes from views in two directions alone?
x-m-fill-b-04.topic: Reasoning about solids with stacked cubes
x-m-fill-b-04.goal: Separate what can and cannot be decided from the top and front views alone, and build cube arrangements that meet the conditions.
x-m-fill-b-04.material: Cubes are stacked on a 2×2 grid, with at least one cube on every spot. The arrangement seen from above is as follows. Back row: left c, right d. Front row: left a, right b. (a, b, c, d are the numbers of levels of cubes stacked on each spot.) The view from the front looks like this: the left vertical column is 3 levels at its tallest, and the right vertical column is 2 levels at its tallest. (When seen from the front, the front row and the back row overlap.)
x-m-fill-b-04.thinking.0: Find the range that the given information decides
x-m-fill-b-04.thinking.1: Make examples that satisfy all the conditions
x-m-fill-b-04.thinking.2: Explain why some cases are impossible
x-m-fill-b-04.prereq.0: Reading the views of stacked cubes from above and from the front
x-m-fill-b-04.prereq.1: That in the same column, the front view shows the highest level
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.prompt: When you know only the view from above and the view from the front, how many stacked cubes in all can you say there are?
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.hint.0: First sort out how many levels the highest level is in each vertical column.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.hint.1: Calculate separately the least and the most you can stack in each column.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.r.a: You looked at only the one case where every spot is stacked as high as possible. Think about whether lower stacks could look the same from the front.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.r.b: You thought only of one cube on each of the 4 spots seen from above and did not use the heights seen from the front.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.r.c: You found the range by considering both the case with the fewest cubes and the case with the most.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.r.d: You looked at only the case with the fewest cubes. Check whether stacking more could look the same.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s1.explain: In the left column, the taller of the two spots is 3 levels and the other spot is at least 1 level, so the least is 3+1, and the right column is 2+1, so there are at least 7 in all. The most is 3+3+2+2=10. Every number from 7 to 10 is possible, so it is not decided as one number.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different ways to stack 8 cubes in all so that the views from above and from the front are the same as described above. (a, b, c, d are the numbers of levels on each spot)
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.hint.0: First write all the possible pairs for the left column (a, c).
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.hint.1: Choose a match where the sum of the left pair and the sum of the right pair add up to 8.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.hint.2: Even if they look similar, like (3,1) and (1,3), they are different ways if the spots are different.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.ok.c1: Every spot has at least 1 level.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.fail.c1: The number of levels on each spot must be an integer that is at least 1.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.ok.c2: The view from the front is the same.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.fail.c2: The maximum of the left column (a, c) must be 3, and the maximum of the right column (b, d) must be 2.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.fail.c3: The number of cubes a+b+c+d is not 8.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s2.explain: There are 6 ways in all to make 8. If the sum of the left column is 4, the sum of the right column is 4, and if the left sum is 5, the right sum is 3. Examples: (a, b, c, d) = (3,2,1,2), (3,2,2,1), (2,2,3,1).
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.prompt: A friend said, 'A shape with 11 stacked cubes is possible too.' Write whether it is possible or not and why.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.hint.0: Reread how many levels the highest level is in each vertical column.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.hint.1: Find the sum when every spot is stacked up to that height.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say what limit the heights seen from the front put on each spot?
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you check with numbers like '3+3+2+2'?
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you avoid confusing it with the case that has the fewest cubes?
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.model.0: You can't make 11. The heights seen from the front are 3 and 2, so no spot can be stacked higher than that, and even stacking the most gives 3+3+2+2=10.
x-m-fill-b-04.s.s3.model.1: Even stacking every spot as high as possible, 10 is the limit, so stacking 11 would change the view from the front.

x-m-fill-b-05.title: Do the conditions alone decide a single triangle?
x-m-fill-b-05.topic: Construction and congruence conditions of triangles
x-m-fill-b-05.goal: Judge whether given side and angle conditions decide one triangle, and explain in the language of construction a case where two triangles are possible.
x-m-fill-b-05.material: Mina wants to construct triangle ABC knowing one of the following conditions. (How to read: ∠A is 'angle A,' and AB is the length of 'segment AB.')
x-m-fill-b-05.thinking.0: Judge whether a condition is sufficient
x-m-fill-b-05.thinking.1: Explain with a construction a counterexample that is not decided
x-m-fill-b-05.prereq.0: Moving segments and angles with a ruler and compass
x-m-fill-b-05.prereq.1: Reading the names of the sides and angles of a triangle
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.prompt: Choose everything among the following where knowing just one condition decides triangle ABC as one triangle.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.hint.0: For each condition, picture where the sides and angles are in relation to each other, as if you were drawing it.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.hint.1: If you suspect it isn't decided, think about whether you can actually draw two with a ruler and compass.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.r.a: You need the habit of checking whether a triangle can be made even when you know the three side lengths (whether the sum of two sides is greater than the other).
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.r.b: Look at whether the angle is between two sides, the positions of the sides and the angle.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.r.c: Think about whether knowing only the angles decides the shape but also decides the size.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.r.d: You know one side and the two angles at both its ends.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.r.e: You know two sides and the angle between them.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s1.explain: a: 3+4>6, so three sides decide one triangle. d: one side and the two angles at its ends decide one. e: two sides and the angle between them decide one. For b, ∠A is not the angle between AB and BC, so two are possible, and for c, there are infinitely many similar triangles of different sizes.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.prompt: For b (AB=6cm, BC=4cm, ∠A=30°), the triangle is not decided as one. Follow the order of construction and explain why.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.hint.0: First draw a ray that makes 30° at A, and picture where the points 4cm away from B lie.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.hint.1: Open the compass to 4cm and draw an arc centered at B. Think about how many times it meets the ray.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you explain which line you drew first from A?
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you write how to find with the compass the places where point C can be?
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you explain the conclusion 'two places' in words without a picture?
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.model.0: Draw a ray that makes 30° at A, and open the compass to 4cm and draw an arc centered at B, and it meets the ray at two places. So C is possible in two places, and there are two triangles.
x-m-fill-b-05.s.s2.model.1: If you measure BC=4, there are 2 points on the ray that C can be. 4cm is longer than the shortest distance from B to the ray (about 3cm), so points appear on both sides.

x-m-fill-b-06.title: If you walk 3 across and 4 up, is the straight-line distance 7?
x-m-fill-b-06.topic: Pythagorean theorem and the distance between two points
x-m-fill-b-06.goal: See the distance between two points as the hypotenuse of a right triangle, find and fix the wrong line in a solution, and find points with integer coordinates at a fixed distance from the origin.
x-m-fill-b-06.material: On a coordinate plane, point A is (1, 2) and point B is (4, 6). (How to read: A is 'horizontal position 1, vertical position 2.') Jimin found the straight-line distance from A to B as follows.
x-m-fill-b-06.thinking.0: Find the wrong line in a solution
x-m-fill-b-06.thinking.2: Find points that meet a condition yourself
x-m-fill-b-06.prereq.0: What the hypotenuse of a right triangle is
x-m-fill-b-06.prereq.1: Reading the position of a point on a coordinate plane as (x, y)
x-m-fill-b-06.prereq.2: Having learned the relationship among the three side lengths of a right triangle
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s1.hint.0: Follow, one by one, whether each line is a conclusion that comes from the line right before it.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s1.line.0: From A to B, they are 4−1=3 apart horizontally and 6−2=4 apart vertically.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s1.line.1: If you make a right triangle with horizontal 3 and vertical 4 as its two sides, the straight-line distance between A and B is its hypotenuse.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s1.line.2: Hypotenuse = 3 + 4 = 7, so the distance between A and B is 7.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s1.line.3: So if you go straight from A to B, you walk 7.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s1.explain: The problem is in line 3, where the hypotenuse was found as the sum of the two sides, and line 4 is its conclusion. For the hypotenuse of a right triangle, (hypotenuse)²=3²+4²=9+16=25, so it is 5. Going 3 horizontally and then 4 vertically is a length of 7, and going straight is shorter than that, 5.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.prompt: Tell Jimin the correct distance and explain why it can't be 7.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.hint.0: First find the sum of the square of the horizontal and the square of the vertical.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what 7 is the combined length of.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you show how you got the distance 5?
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say what 7 is the length of (the roundabout path)?
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you write why the straight line is shorter than the roundabout path?
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.model.0: The distance is 5. The hypotenuse squared is 3²+4²=9+16=25, so the hypotenuse is 5. 3+4=7 is the path going horizontally and then vertically, and the straight line is shorter than that.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s2.model.1: 7 is wrong. Adding the lengths of the two sides gives the roundabout path, not the hypotenuse of the right triangle. The hypotenuse² is 25, so the distance is 5.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s3.prompt: This time, find points P(a, b) whose distance from the origin O(0, 0) is exactly 13. Find 3 different points whose coordinates are all integers. (a and b can be 0 or negative.)
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s3.hint.0: The square of the distance is 169. Find pairs of square numbers that add up to 169.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s3.hint.1: Change a from 0 to 13 and check whether b²=169−a² is a square number.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s3.fail.c1: a and b must be integers.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s3.ok.c2: The distance from the origin is 13.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s3.fail.c2: a²+b² is not 169. The distance is not 13.
x-m-fill-b-06.s.s3.explain: The distance from the origin to point (a, b) is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with horizontal |a| and vertical |b| as its two sides, so a²+b²=13²=169. Examples: (5,12), (12,5), (0,13), (−5,12), and so on.

x-m-fill-b-07.title: Checking addition answers by estimating
x-m-fill-b-07.goal: Use estimation to rule out a wrong answer, explain why regrouping was left out, and make addition expressions with regrouping yourself.
x-m-fill-b-07.material: Seojin, Hana, and Daon calculated 38+27. Seojin: 55, Hana: 65, Daon: 75. The teacher told them, '38 is less than 40 and 27 is less than 30. 40+30 is 70.'
x-m-fill-b-07.thinking.1: Explain why an answer is wrong
x-m-fill-b-07.thinking.2: Make an expression that meets conditions
x-m-fill-b-07.prereq.0: The tens place and the ones place of a two-digit number
x-m-fill-b-07.prereq.1: Carrying to the tens place when it reaches 10
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.prompt: Whose answer can you say for sure is wrong by estimation alone?
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.hint.0: First write what number each of 38 and 27 is less than.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.hint.1: If you add those two numbers, 38+27 is less than what?
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.r.a: 65 is less than 70, so you can't say it is wrong by estimation.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.r.b: 38 and 27 are less than 40 and 30, so the sum must be less than 70.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.r.c: 55 is less than 70 even by estimation, so it is hard to say it is wrong.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.o.d: Estimation can't rule out even one wrong answer
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.r.d: With estimation you can find answers that are bigger than 70. Think about what estimation is useful for.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s1.explain: 38 is less than 40 and 27 is less than 30, so the sum is less than 70. 75 is more than 70, so it is wrong. 55 and 65 can't be ruled out by estimation alone.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.prompt: Of the two remaining answers 55 and 65, explain, starting from the ones place, why Seojin's answer (55) is wrong.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.hint.0: Imagine how Seojin may have written the sum of the ones place.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.hint.1: What happens to the tens place when the sum of the ones place goes over 10?
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say how 8+7=15 in the ones place is written?
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you say why 1 is added to 3+2 in the tens place?
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you check that the correct answer is 65?
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.model.0: In the ones place, 8+7=15, but I forgot to carry 10 to the tens place. The tens place is 3+2+1=6, so 65 is right.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s2.model.1: 8 and 7 add up to 15, so there is 1 more ten block. It should have been added to the tens place, but it wasn't. So 65 is right.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.prompt: Make 3 different addition expressions of two-digit numbers where the ones digits add to more than 10 and the sum is at least 60 and less than 70. (Write the two numbers you add as a and b. Swapping a and b is the same expression.)
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.hint.0: If the ones digits are big, regrouping happens. First think of pairs that add to more than 10, like 8 and 7.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.hint.1: Check that the sum including the tens place is in the 60s.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.fail.c1: a and b are integers from 10 to 99.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.ok.c2: The ones digits add to more than 10.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.fail.c2: The ones digits do not add to more than 10. There is no regrouping.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.ok.c3: The sum is at least 60 and less than 70.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.fail.c3: The sum is not at least 60 and less than 70.
x-m-fill-b-07.s.s3.explain: Examples: 38+27=65 (8+7=15), 19+48=67 (9+8=17), 25+36=61 (5+6=11). If the sum of the ones digits is 10 to 18 and the whole sum is 60 to 69, the sum of the tens digits is 5.

x-m-fill-b-08.title: Squaring and comparing with 7: which is bigger?
x-m-fill-b-08.goal: Find and fix the wrong line in a solution that compares a square root and a decimal by squaring, and find numbers between two numbers yourself.
x-m-fill-b-08.material: Jiho solved which of √7 and 2.6 is bigger as follows. (√7 is read 'root seven.' It is the positive number that gives 7 when squared.)
x-m-fill-b-08.thinking.0: Find the wrong line in a solution
x-m-fill-b-08.thinking.1: Connect the comparison of squared values to the comparison of the original numbers
x-m-fill-b-08.thinking.2: Make numbers that meet a condition
x-m-fill-b-08.prereq.0: The meaning of square root (the positive number that gives that number when squared)
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s1.prompt: Choose the wrong line in Jiho's solution. (If several lines are wrong, you only need to choose one of them.)
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s1.hint.0: Put the 6.76 in line 2 and the squared value of √7 side by side and compare them.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check with numbers (for example 2 and 3) whether, for positive numbers, the one with the smaller square is also the smaller original number.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the problem, and line 4 is its conclusion. For positive numbers, the one with the smaller square is the smaller number. 2.6²=6.76 is less than (√7)²=7, so 2.6 is less than √7. So √7 > 2.6.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.prompt: This time, find 3 different numbers x, written to the second decimal place, that are greater than √7 and less than 2.7. (2.7²=7.29)
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.hint.0: Check one by one whether the square of x is greater than 7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.ok.c1: A positive number to the second decimal place.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.fail.c1: x must be a positive number to the second decimal place. (e.g. 2.65)
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.ok.c2: x² is greater than 7, so x is greater than √7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.fail.c2: x² is not greater than 7. x is not greater than √7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.ok.c3: x² is less than 7.29, so x is less than 2.7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.fail.c3: x² is not less than 7.29. x is not less than 2.7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.explain: 2.65²=7.0225, 2.67²=7.1289, and 2.69²=7.2361 are all greater than 7 and less than 7.29. 2.64²=6.9696<7, so 2.64 is less than √7. The real √7 is about 2.6458.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.prompt: Write why you can say 2.65 is greater than √7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.hint.0: Start with a sentence that squares x and compares it with 7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.hint.1: Check with numbers (for example 2 and 3) why, when you square two numbers, the one with the bigger square is also the bigger original number.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you find the squared value and compare it with 7?
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write that for positive numbers, the bigger the square, the bigger the original number?
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you write the reason instead of just copying a calculator result?
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.model.0: For x to be greater than √7, the square of x must be greater than 7. 2.65²=7.0225>7, so 2.65>√7.
x-m-fill-b-08.s.s2.because.model.1: For positive numbers, the bigger the square, the bigger the original number. Squaring 2.65 gives 7.0225, which is greater than 7, so 2.65 is greater than √7.

x-m-fill-b-09.title: Is the fraction with the bigger numerator bigger?
x-m-fill-b-09.goal: Compare the sizes of fractions with a method you can trust, and show with examples you make yourself that 'a bigger numerator means a bigger fraction' is not always true.
x-m-fill-b-09.material: Yunseo wants to compare the sizes of 3/8 and 2/3. (3/8 is read 'three eighths,' and 2/3 is read 'two thirds.') Minho said, 'The fraction with the bigger numerator is the bigger fraction.'
x-m-fill-b-09.thinking.0: Pick out comparison methods you can trust
x-m-fill-b-09.thinking.2: Explain the relationship between denominator and numerator
x-m-fill-b-09.prereq.0: The meaning of a fraction (some pieces out of a whole divided into equal parts)
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.prompt: Choose every method you can trust to find out which of 3/8 and 2/3 is bigger.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.hint.0: Actually compare 3/8 and 2/3 with each method and check whether the results are the same.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.hint.1: Think of examples to see whether a method that looks at only the numerator or only the denominator works for other fractions too.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.o.a: Treat the one with the bigger numerator as the bigger fraction
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.r.a: For fractions you have to look at the numerator and the denominator together. A method that compares only numerators can't be trusted.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.o.b: Make the denominators the same with a common denominator and compare the numerators
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.r.b: When the denominators are the same, you can compare the numbers of equal-sized pieces.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.o.c: Compare each with 1/2 to see whether it is bigger or smaller
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.r.c: You try to place the two fractions by comparing them with a benchmark fraction.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.o.d: Treat the one with the bigger denominator as the smaller fraction
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.r.d: A bigger denominator makes each piece smaller, but the number of pieces also differs, so this method alone can't decide.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s1.explain: b: With a common denominator, 3/8=9/24 and 2/3=16/24, so 2/3 is bigger. c: 3/8 is less than 1/2 and 2/3 is greater than 1/2, so 2/3 is bigger. a and d look at only the numerator or only the denominator, so they can't be trusted.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.prompt: Minho's statement is not always true. Make 3 different examples where the fraction with the bigger numerator is actually the smaller fraction. For proper fractions a/b and c/d, a must be greater than c but a/b must be less than c/d. (Numerators and denominators are natural numbers from 1 to 12.)
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.hint.0: If the denominators differ a lot, the fraction can be smaller even when the numerator is bigger.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.hint.1: Check the two fractions you made by finding a common denominator or comparing them with 1/2.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The numerators and denominators must be natural numbers from 1 to 12.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.fail.c2: The numerator must be less than the denominator. (proper fraction)
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.ok.c3: The numerator of a/b is bigger.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.fail.c3: a is not greater than c.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.fail.c4: a/b is not less than c/d.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.explain: Examples: 3/8<2/3 (3>2), 5/9<4/5 (5>4), 2/7<1/2 (2>1). Even if the numerator is bigger, if the denominator is much bigger, the whole was cut into smaller parts, so each piece is smaller.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.prompt: Pick one of the examples you just made and explain why the fraction is smaller even though its numerator is bigger.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.hint.0: Say how many pieces each denominator cuts the whole into.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.hint.1: Write what happens when you find a common denominator for the two fractions you chose.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you write the pair of fractions you chose specifically?
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you write that a bigger denominator makes the pieces smaller?
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you check with a common denominator or with decimals?
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.model.0: In 3/8 and 2/3, the numerator 3 is bigger, but the denominator is also 8, so each piece is smaller. With a common denominator they are 9/24 and 16/24, so 2/3 is bigger.
x-m-fill-b-09.s.s2.because.model.1: Even if the numerator is bigger, if the denominator is much bigger, the whole is cut into small parts, so each piece is small. 5/9 is about 0.56 and 4/5 is 0.8.
